strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: reducing hallucination in statement autoformalization by improving retrieval of formal library dependencies.

Proposes a novel generation-plus-verification RAG paradigm (DDR) where an LLM directly generates candidate dependencies and a suffix-array check verifies their existence, avoiding embedding-based retrieval and a pre-specified number of dependencies.

Constructs a large-scale dependency retrieval dataset from FineLeanCorpus (500k+ samples) and states it is open-sourced, which could be useful for future work on autoformalization and formal library retrieval.
The suffix-array verification method is simple, efficient, and scalable in principle, with O(sM log N) query complexity and demonstrated processing of the entire corpus in under two hours.
Experiments show consistent improvements in retrieval F1 and downstream BEq-based autoformalization compared to R@5/R@10 baselines, plus additional multi-attempt consistency and efficiency analyses.
The paper is generally clear, well motivated, and relevant to computational linguistics and NLP, especially at the intersection of LLMs, retrieval, and formal mathematics.
weaknesses: The retrieval evaluation uses a suffix-component matching criterion that may treat ambiguous unqualified names as correct, potentially inflating precision and recall; the paper itself notes that DDR cannot precisely locate generated items due to abbreviated names.

The baseline comparison is narrow: retrieval is compared mainly against R@5/R@10 from one prior method, with no comparison to standard sparse/dense retrievers, rerankers, or alternative verification strategies, making the 'SOTA' claim less convincing.
Test sets are small (roughly 200 statements per difficulty split), and no statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are reported, so the observed gains may be noisy.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the open-source dataset link is not visible in the manuscript, no code or fine-tuned model release is mentioned, and key evaluation details (BEq procedure, baseline R@k implementation) rely on external work.
The method is incompatible with the existing RAG autoformalizer framework because required metadata fields are set to None; this may limit practical deployment and makes the comparison less clean.
TypeC scores for RA+DDR remain below those of several ICL baselines, suggesting that many generated formal statements may still fail to typecheck despite improved BEq scores.
Generalizability beyond FineLeanCorpus is not demonstrated, and the suffix-array matching ambiguity may become more problematic on larger or more complex formal libraries such as full Mathlib.

Several methodological details are underspecified, including how dependency labels are extracted from formal code, how exact/partial/none matches are defined, and how the suffix array handles qualified names and delimiters robustly.

strengths: The paper tackles a relevant and challenging problem in autoformalization: retrieving correct formal-library dependencies from informal mathematical statements. This is a key bottleneck for scaling retrieval-augmented autoformalization.

The proposed DDR paradigm is simple and intuitive: use an LLM to generate candidate dependencies directly from the informal statement, then verify existence in the formal library with a suffix-array lookup. This avoids some limitations of embedding-based retrieval and does not require a pre-specified number of dependencies.
The suffix-array verification is efficient and well-motivated. The O(log N) lookup claim is plausible for existence checks, and the method enables large-scale dataset construction.
The paper constructs and plans to open-source a dependency-retrieval dataset with over 500k samples, which is a valuable resource for the community.

The experiments cover multiple difficulty subsets, several ICL and SFT baselines, retrieval metrics, downstream autoformalization metrics, and multi-attempt consistency/efficiency analyses. This is a reasonably broad empirical study.

The results are promising: DDR substantially outperforms R@5/R@10 retrieval baselines in Table 2, and RA+DDR generally improves over RA and RA+R@k on downstream TypeC and BEq, especially on harder subsets.
The paper is generally clear, with helpful diagrams (e.g., Figure 1 and Figure 2) that explain the selection-based vs. generation-plus-verification paradigms.
The discussion section is relatively honest about a key limitation: DDR generates abbreviated names and is not directly compatible with frameworks that expect full metadata.
The training details (LoRA, learning rate, batch size, epochs, prompt reuse from prior work) provide a reasonable starting point for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The main empirical comparison is confounded. DDR is fine-tuned on ~500k in-domain dependency pairs and uses Qwen3-32B, while the retrieval baselines are not fine-tuned on the same dependency data and the RA baseline uses a 7B InternLM2-Math model. The large gains may come from supervised in-domain training and model size rather than from the DDR paradigm itself. A fair comparison should fine-tune an embedding-based retriever on the same data or use the same base model for RA and DDR.

The suffix-array verification only checks whether a generated identifier exists in the library, not whether it is relevant to the statement. Thus the 'generation-plus-verification' framing overstates the verification step: it filters hallucinations but cannot correct semantically wrong dependencies.

The retrieval evaluation uses a lenient suffix-based matching criterion. Because DDR outputs unqualified or abbreviated names, this criterion may over-credit partial matches and inflate precision/recall. Exact-match or manually validated metrics are needed to substantiate the high precision/recall claims.

The handling of samples with no ground-truth dependencies is unclear. Diff01 has a low dependency rate (0.20 for difficulty 0), so retrieval metrics may be distorted if empty ground truths are included or excluded inconsistently. The paper should report results on samples with dependencies and clarify how empty cases are scored.

The dependency extraction procedure is under-specified. It is not clear whether dependencies are extracted from formal statements, full proofs, or both; how local variables and non-library identifiers are filtered; and how the suffix-array check is used to produce labels. This directly affects dataset quality and reproducibility.

There is no ablation isolating the contribution of suffix-array verification from the fine-tuned LLM generation. The paper does not compare against a fine-tuned LLM without verification, nor against a fine-tuned embedding retriever, so the source of improvement remains ambiguous.

Generalization is not demonstrated. All experiments use FineLeanCorpus, and the test sets are from the same corpus/distribution used for training. Claims about scalability and applicability to other formal corpora are not empirically supported.

Inference efficiency is not evaluated. The suffix array is fast, but DDR requires generation with a 32B LLM, which is likely much slower than embedding retrieval. The paper's 'real-time' and scalability claims therefore need runtime/latency comparisons.

Reproducibility is limited by missing artifacts: the open-source dataset URL appears blank, no code is provided, and the Lean/Mathlib, Qwen3, and DeepSeek-Prover versions are not specified. The dependency extraction script is also not described in enough detail.

No statistical significance tests are reported. Test sets contain only 200 samples per subset, and several reported differences (e.g., Diff23 and Diff45 TypeC/BEq) are small enough that they could be noise. Claims such as 'significantly outperforms' are not statistically supported.

Potential pretraining contamination is not discussed. Qwen3-32B may have seen Lean/Mathlib code during pretraining, which could give DDR an advantage in generating dependency names. This should be checked or controlled.

The paper does not analyze the failure mode where DDR is much worse than ICL models on Diff01 (e.g., BEq 0.32 vs. 0.61 for Claude-3.5-Sonnet). Understanding and mitigating this would strengthen the contribution.
No systematic error analysis is provided for DDR. It would be useful to know when generation+verification succeeds or fails, and what types of dependencies are missed or hallucinated.

The MMA baseline is mentioned without a citation, and the related work does not discuss generative retrieval methods that also directly generate document identifiers. This affects novelty positioning.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and important problem: hallucination and low accuracy in formal-library dependency retrieval, which is a genuine bottleneck for autoformalization.

The suffix-array-based verification mechanism is technically clean and gives an explicit efficiency argument (O(sM log N) matching vs. brute-force O((s+d)MN)), enabling scalable dataset construction and real-time verification.
Constructs and releases a large-scale (500K+ samples) dependency-retrieval dataset derived from FineLeanCorpus, which could be a useful resource for the community.

The experimental suite is reasonably broad, including several strong LLM baselines (DeepSeek-R1, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, GPT-4o, Qwen2.5-Max) plus ablations on multi-attempt consistency and generation efficiency.
Clearly articulates the intended design of DDR (generation-plus-verification) and contrasts it with embedding-based selection, with an informative qualitative illustration in Figure 1.
weaknesses: Retrieval evaluation is methodologically questionable: the ground-truth dependency labels are themselves extracted from formal source code via the same suffix-array mechanism, and the true-positive criterion (suffix/component matching) is loose, so precision/recall largely measure agreement with a heuristic extraction rather than semantic dependency necessity.

The R@5/R@10 embedding-retrieval baselines show implausibly low precision (0.03–0.12). With no detail on the embedding model, index, tuning, or configuration, this looks like a strawman and undercuts the claim of 'significant' improvement.

Downstream gains are modest and inconsistent. In Table 3, DDR does not consistently beat strong ICL models (e.g., Claude-3.5-Sonnet) on BEq/TypeC across subsets, and on Diff01 the improvement over RA+R@5 is marginal, which is weaker than the paper's framing suggests.
Reproducibility gaps: the dataset is stated to be 'open-source at [blank]' — the URL is missing; the R@k baseline setup and the exact DDR training-data construction are under-specified.

Comparison fairness is unclear: DDR is fine-tuned on data drawn from the same corpus as the evaluation, the autoformalizer differs across conditions, and potential train/test overlap at the dependency-pattern level is not addressed.

Limited novelty: generation-plus-verification is a known paradigm; the main technical contribution (suffix-array verification) is essentially an efficiency/engineering addition rather than a conceptual advance.

Claims are overstated relative to the evidence ('significantly outperforms SOTA'), and there is no systematic error analysis; the acknowledged limitation (no metadata/qualified-name retrieval) is described but never quantified.

strengths: Addresses an important bottleneck in autoformalization: retrieval of correct formal dependencies and hallucination of non-existent Mathlib objects.
Proposes DDR, a generation-plus-verification retrieval framework, and SAC, an efficient suffix-array verification method that can be plugged into both ICL and SFT autoformalization pipelines.

Constructs and claims to open-source a large-scale dependency retrieval dataset with over 500k samples derived from FineLeanCorpus, which could support future research on dependency-aware autoformalization.
Provides extensive experiments across multiple LLMs, difficulty subsets, retrieval precision/recall, hallucination rates, and downstream TypeC/BEq pass@k metrics.
Empirically demonstrates consistent relative gains: DDR retrieval precision/recall outperforms ICL and R@k baselines, and DDR-augmented autoformalizers generally improve over non-DDR variants.
Introduces a quantitative hallucination analysis for dependency retrieval and proposes Depend Rate/Length as difficulty proxies, which are useful diagnostic signals.
Includes a limitations section that acknowledges some practical constraints, such as abbreviated dependency names and library evolution.
weaknesses: The core verification metric is potentially too lenient: SAC uses suffix/partial and dot-component-subset matching, so generated identifiers that are merely substrings or component subsets of real library objects may be counted as valid. This can inflate retrieval precision/recall and underestimate hallucination rates, weakening the central claims.

Reproducibility is limited: the manuscript says the dataset is open-access but provides no actual link, and there is no clear code/model release. The paper relies on prompts and hyperparameters but not enough to fully reproduce the pipeline.

The construction of the 500k-sample training dataset and dependency labels is not fully specified. It is unclear how dependencies are extracted from formal code, how candidate items are verified, and how label noise or train/test leakage is controlled.

The downstream comparison with RA+DDR is confounded by a format mismatch: DDR outputs only abbreviated dependency names, whereas the RA autoformalizer expects full dependency metadata. The reported gains may therefore reflect experimental setup choices rather than purely better retrieval.

Absolute downstream performance remains low (e.g., BEq pass@8 often below 0.3), and gains are modest. No statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are reported, making it difficult to judge whether small differences are meaningful.
The evaluation is limited to one corpus (FineLeanCorpus) and one prover/library (Lean/Mathlib). Generalization to other formal libraries, provers, or mathematical domains is not demonstrated.

The claim that SAC provides a sound mechanism for assessing formalization difficulty and overcomes subjectivity/stochasticity of LLM graders is overstated. The proposed difficulty proxies are not validated against human expert judgments.

The novelty of SAC is limited: it applies standard suffix-array exact/partial string matching to library identifiers, and the paper does not compare against other verification or retrieval strategies such as exact-match checks, BM25, or dense retrieval beyond the selected baselines.

strengths: Addresses an important and difficult problem in autoformalization: retrieving the correct Mathlib dependencies from informal mathematical statements, where hallucinated dependencies are a major source of failure.

Proposes a simple and effective generation-plus-verification paradigm (DDR + SAC). DDR directly generates candidate dependencies from context, and SAC provides efficient suffix-array-based existence verification, avoiding reliance on embedding similarity over a large formal library.
Constructs and plans to release a large-scale dependency retrieval dataset with over 500,000 samples, which is a valuable resource for the formal mathematics and autoformalization communities.

Provides comprehensive experiments across multiple difficulty subsets, multiple LLMs (Claude-3.5-Sonnet, DeepSeek-R1, GPT-4o, Ling-flash-2.0, Qwen-Max), and both SFT and ICL settings. DDR consistently improves retrieval precision/recall and downstream BEq/TypeC performance.

Quantifies hallucination in ICL-based dependency retrieval, showing that prompt-based methods hallucinate roughly 30% of dependencies, while DDR's hallucination rate is below 0.02 after SAC verification. This is a useful diagnostic contribution.
Demonstrates that DDR can be used as a plug-and-play retrieval module in both ICL and SFT autoformalization pipelines, improving over RA+R@5 and RA+R@10 baselines.
Provides detailed reproducibility information in the appendix, including hyperparameters, base model, training framework, prompt templates, and evaluation metrics.
The Depend Rate and Depend Length analysis offers an interesting alternative to LLM-assigned difficulty scores, and the resulting difficulty ranking aligns with some experimental observations.
weaknesses: No statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are reported. Many downstream BEq differences are small (e.g., 0.105 vs. 0.095, 0.065 vs. 0.055), and test sets contain only 200 statements with 8 samples per problem, so the reported gains may be within noise.

Semantic equivalence is evaluated only via TypeC and BEq using an auxiliary prover (DeepSeek-Prover-v2), with no human evaluation or validation of BEq on the reported test sets. Since BEq is central to the main autoformalization claims, this limits confidence in the semantic fidelity conclusions.

The retrieval precision/recall metric uses a custom suffix/dot-component substring matching criterion because DDR emits abbreviated names. This may be lenient and can over-credit partially qualified or related names; false positives/negatives are not analyzed in detail.

There is a potential circularity: SAC is used both to construct training labels from formal code and to verify/filter model outputs, including the hallucination rate. The correctness and coverage of SAC are not independently validated, so both retrieval quality and hallucination estimates depend on the same verification mechanism.

The comparison is not fully controlled for base-model capacity. DDR is fine-tuned on Qwen3-32B, while the RA baseline is based on a 7B model and prompt-based baselines are not fine-tuned on the same dependency data. Some gains may reflect model scale and fine-tuning rather than the DDR paradigm itself.

Evaluation is in-distribution: training and test sets are drawn from the same FineLeanCorpus, and there is no cross-library, cross-corpus, or out-of-distribution evaluation. The scalability and generalization claims are therefore not fully tested.

Ablations are limited. The paper does not isolate the effect of SAC at inference (generation-only vs. generation+verification), does not vary training data size, and does not compare against a fine-tuned generative retrieval baseline using the same base model.

DDR outputs only abbreviated dependency names rather than full metadata, which limits compatibility with existing retrieval-augmented autoformalizers such as RA. This is acknowledged but not fully resolved.

The difficulty analysis is only based on Depend Rate/Length, excludes Diff01, and is not validated against expert judgments. It is presented as a potential indicator rather than a rigorously established metric.
The open-access dataset link appears incomplete in the manuscript, and no code release is mentioned, which may hinder reproducibility despite the otherwise detailed hyperparameters.

Absolute autoformalization performance remains low (BEq mostly below 0.3, often below 0.1), so the practical impact on formal verification workflows is uncertain even though relative improvements are consistent.
Minor presentation issues: some tables and figures are dense/small, and there are small typos (e.g., stray 'y' in Table 2 caption), though overall clarity is acceptable.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: improving dependency retrieval for autoformalization to reduce LLM hallucination in formal mathematics.

It proposes a generation-plus-verification framework (DDR + SAC) and constructs a large-scale dependency retrieval dataset from FineLeanCorpus (>500k samples), with prompt templates and training hyperparameters documented.
The experiments cover multiple difficulty splits, compare against ICL and retrieval baselines, and evaluate both retrieval metrics and downstream autoformalization using TypeC and BEq.
SAC is an efficient suffix-array-based string matching component with potential for dataset construction and hallucination quantification.
The paper discusses limitations and is relevant to NLP/CL communities working on formal reasoning and autoformalization.
weaknesses: The core SAC verification is not sound for hallucination prevention: suffix-array substring matching can accept non-existent partial identifiers (e.g., 'Nat.foo' inside 'Nat.foobar'), so 'existence verification' does not guarantee exact library object existence. This undermines the central hallucination claims and dataset quality.

There is an unresolved inconsistency: DDR with SAC verification should produce zero hallucination, yet Table 2 reports nonzero rates; it is unclear whether DDR outputs are pre- or post-verification, or whether partial matches are counted as hallucinations.

Retrieval comparisons are not apples-to-apples: DDR is fine-tuned on 500k samples, while R@5/R@10 and ICL baselines are zero-shot or not trained on the same data. The paper does not control for this, so claimed superiority may be due to additional supervision/compute.

Dataset labels are extracted from FineLeanCorpus formal statements, which may contain LLM-generated errors; SAC checks only existence, not relevance, and no human validation is reported. The 'high-quality' dataset claim is therefore not fully supported.

The downstream RA+DDR experiment is unclear: DDR outputs only abbreviated dependency names, while RA requires full metadata (name, description, code). The authors acknowledge this mismatch but do not explain how integration works, so gains may not be attributable to DDR retrieval.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the dataset URL appears missing/blank in the manuscript, no code release is mentioned, and there are no significance tests or confidence intervals; some downstream improvements are small and could be noise.

The method's novelty is limited: suffix-array string matching is standard, and the overall pipeline (fine-tuned LLM generation + filtering) is a straightforward combination. Baselines are also limited (e.g., no comparison to LeanDojo/ReProver or other dependency retrieval methods).

The difficulty analysis using Depend Rate/Length is circular and not independently validated; it excludes Diff01 and relies on the same DDR/SAC metrics to rank difficulty. Writing/clarity issues (typos, undefined 'authentic', malformed references) further reduce rigor.
